Draft:
"Insulation slows heat transfer primarily by manipulating conduction, convection, and radiation. Heat moves from high-temperature component to lower-temperature surroundings via these mechanisms. In conduction, Fourier’s law states heat flux is proportional to thermal conductivity and temperature gradient, inversely proportional to material thickness: q = -kAΔT/L. Insulation materials have low thermal conductivity (e.g., foams, fiberglass, aerogels) and often trap low-conductivity gas or fibrous air spaces. This raises effective thermal resistance R = L/k, so for same ΔT, less heat flows per area.

Convection is reduced when insulation fills air gaps and irregular surfaces, interrupting direct fluid paths and creating more boundary layers. Still air is poor conductor; trapped air lowers effective conductivity. Radiation can be reduced with low-emissivity coatings or reflective barriers that lower surface emissivity/absorptivity, though insulation mainly addresses conduction/convection.

In a GPU, thermal pads, case walls, or heatsink designs act as insulation layers between hot die and cooler or between components. They don't eliminate heat transfer; they increase thermal resistance and lower steady-state heat flux, raising thermal resistance. This means temperature rises more slowly for a given heat load, but equilibrium temperature still depends on heat generation and cooling capacity. Over time, if heat buildup exceeds limits, throttling or shutdown occurs."
